pois.description:en: A small, charming hobbit door in Bellevue Botanical Garden originally built as an entrance to a root cellar owned by Cal and Harriet Shorts. It now serves as a whimsical feature that delights visitors exploring the garden's wooded trails.
pois.description:es: Pequeña y encantadora puerta en el Bellevue Botanical Garden, construida originalmente como entrada a una bodega de Cal y Harriet Shorts. Ahora es un detalle caprichoso que encanta a los visitantes.
pois.description:fr: Petite porte charmante dans le Bellevue Botanical Garden, construite à l'origine comme entrée d'une cave à racines appartenant à Cal et Harriet Shorts. Aujourd'hui, c'est une attraction fantaisiste qui enchante les visiteurs.
pois.description:ja: ベルビュー植物園にある小さく魅力的なホビットのドアで、元々はカルとハリエット・ショーツ夫妻が所有していた貯蔵室の入口として建てられました。現在は、庭園の木立の中の小径を探索する訪問者を楽しませる幻想的な特徴となっています。
pois.description:ko: 벨뷰 식물원에 있는 작고 매력적인 호빗 문으로, 원래는 칼과 해리엇 쇼츠가 소유했던 지하 저장고 입구로 지어졌습니다. 현재는 정원의 숲길을 탐험하는 방문객들을 즐겁게 하는 기발한 특징으로 자리 잡고 있습니다.
pois.description:zh: 贝尔维尤植物园内一扇小巧迷人的霍比特人门，最初建作为Cal和Harriet Shorts拥有的地窖入口。如今，它成为了一个充满奇幻色彩的特色，为探索花园树林小径的游客带来欢愉。

bel-botanical-garden.name: Bellevue Botanical Garden
bel-botanical-garden.blurb: 53 free acres of Pacific Northwest gardens: the Perennial Border, the Yao Japanese garden, a suspension bridge over the ravine and the winter Garden d'Lights.

spawn.note: Outside the Shorts Visitor Center courtyard at the start of the Tateuchi Loop.

extent.description: Core garden: visitor center, Perennial Border, Rock/Waterwise gardens, Urban Meadow, Yao Garden, Fuchsia garden, Lost Meadow Trail, the Ravine Experience suspension bridge.
extent.edges: Forest of Wilburton Hill Park around; Main St entrance north.
extent.vertical: Hilly; ravine drops ~15 m under the suspension bridge (estimate; see terrain).

structures.name: Yao Garden
structures.form: Japanese-style garden honouring sister city Yao, Japan: stream, maples, azaleas, rhododendrons, a gate/entry and lantern.

structures.name: Perennial Border (Northwest Perennial Alliance)
structures.form: Long sweeping beds of perennials, bulbs, grasses and shrubs along paths and steps — "largest public perennial garden in America" per Wikipedia.

vegetation: Dense mixed conifer forest (Douglas fir, western red cedar, big-leaf maple) around
Seasonal: rhododendrons (May), dahlias (Aug–Sep), Japanese maple colour (Oct)
furniture: 73 benches, 2 picnic tables, info boards (4), toilets (OSM)

lighting.night: Garden d'Lights (late Nov–Dec): plants and flowers sculpted from hundreds of thousands of LED lights (count unverified)

backdrop: Forest; occasional glimpse of downtown Bellevue towers to the west

crowd.density: Low-medium; gardeners, families, photographers; very high on Garden d'Lights evenings.

plaques.title: From a gift
plaques.text: What began as a 7-acre gift from the Shorts family in the early 1980s is now a 53-acre public garden, opened June 27, 1992.

plaques.title: Perennial Border
plaques.text: Maintained by the Northwest Perennial Alliance and volunteers, the Perennial Border is described as the largest public perennial garden in America.

plaques.title: Yao Garden
plaques.text: The Yao Garden celebrates Bellevue's sister city Yao, Japan, with plants from the Pacific Northwest, Japan and the Pacific Rim.

plaques.title: Free
plaques.text: The garden is free and open dawn to dusk.

dialogueGeneral.usage: Pedestrian set for the Seattle and Bellevue driving districts and as filler in every spot. ctx: greeting|bumped|photographed|idle|spot|rain|honked_at|near_miss; non-English lines carry orig+lang with English text.

tone.note: "Seattle Freeze": locals are described as "very polite but not particularly friendly" to strangers — keep local NPC lines courteous, brief, low-key; few unprompted chats.
Washington ranked 48th of 50 states for extraversion (2008 study cited by Wikipedia) — locals default to nods, "sorry", "you're good".

Honking is rare and seen as rude: ~3 in 4 Northwest drivers said they rarely or never honk (PEMCO 2017); attitudes softened by 2021 (65% say honking at least somewhat appropriate). NPC reaction to player honking near spots: surprised/disapproving, not aggressive.
Coffee culture: Seattle drinks more coffee than any other US city; espresso small talk is a safe icebreaker.
Rain talk is universal small talk; locals rarely use umbrellas (hoods/rain shells) — common local self-image, unsourced folklore: keep light.

Visitors: Canada was 73% of Seattle's 2.4 M international visitors in 2024; then China, India, UK, South Korea, Germany, Japan, Australia, France, Taiwan — languages used: English, French (Québec), Mandarin, Hindi, Korean, German, Japanese, Spanish (domestic + Latin America).
Indigenous art (totems, Salish Welcome): staff/guides speak respectfully; no jokes about sacred objects.
Guardrails: no stereotypes, accents written phonetically, slurs, politics or alcohol jokes about any group; tourists are curious and happy, locals helpful-but-reserved.
